# Glossary {#sec-appendix-a}

Each entry gives the book's definition, word for word as it appears where the term is defined, and the chapter that defines it ("also" marks other chapters that list the term among their Key Terms). Labels in parentheses, such as *(of a model)* or *(Deep)*, separate different senses of a word or mark a term from an optional Deep section. A Turkish equivalents index follows the English entries.

## A {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Abstract** · Ch. 9
:   The short summary at the start of a research article.

**Affirmed** · Ch. 18
:   The appeals court agreed with the trial court's decision.

**Agency (mode of working with AI)** · Ch. 5
:   Working with AI in which you configure it to carry out future tasks on your behalf, including for other people. Not the same as an agent.

**Agent** · Ch. 3
:   A system in which the model directs its own steps and tool use toward a goal; in a workflow, people fixed the steps in advance (adapted from Anthropic, 2024). Not the same as the AI Fluency "agency" mode.

**Agent loop** · Ch. 14
:   The cycle an agent repeats: the model produces a plan for the next action, the system runs the tool call, and the result, the observation, is added to the context window, until a stop condition is met.

**AI search** · Ch. 9
:   A tool that retrieves pages and then produces an answer with links (the search-then-generate lane).

**AI tool** · Ch. 12
:   The software you use: a model plus what the tool adds to the model's context window, what it can do, where the model runs and whose terms cover it.

**AI Use Declaration** · Ch. 1
:   A short statement of which AI tools you used, for what, what you accepted, rejected or revised, how you verified it, and where your judgment shaped the work.

**AI Work Loop** · Ch. 1
:   The book's five-step method for AI-assisted work: Frame, Prompt, Verify, Decide, Disclose.

**AI-mediated communication (Deep)** · Ch. 10
:   Communication between people in which software acts on behalf of one of them by changing, adding to or generating their message.

**AI-text detector** · Ch. 10
:   A tool that gives a score for how likely a text is to have been generated by AI.

**Algorithm register** · Ch. 17
:   A public list of the algorithms an organization uses, with their purpose and a contact.

**Allocation harm** · Ch. 16
:   Harm that withholds an opportunity or resource, such as a job or a place in a program.

**Alt text** · Ch. 13
:   A short text alternative for an image that tells a reader who cannot see it what they need to know from it.

**Anatomy of a prompt** · Ch. 5
:   The book's six-part description of what a prompt can contain: role, task, context, constraints, in-context examples and output format.

**Annotated draft** · Ch. 10
:   An AI-assisted draft with every sentence coded keep (K), rewrite (R) or reject (X) and tagged with a reason.

**Answer mode** · Ch. 7
:   The default way of using an AI tool, in which it produces the answer or finished work you ask for.

**Appeals court** · Ch. 18
:   A court that reviews trial courts' decisions in its region (for example, the Third Circuit).

**Appropriate reliance** · Ch. 17
:   Relying on a system when it is right and not relying on it when it is wrong (after Lee & See, 2004).

**Approval fatigue** · Ch. 14
:   Approvals given so often or so quickly that they stop working as checks.

**Approval gate** · Ch. 14
:   A point at which a system pauses before an action takes effect until a named person approves, edits or rejects it.

**Assistance** · Ch. 1
:   AI use that helps you do the thinking yourself.

**Attention (Deep)** · Ch. 3
:   In a Transformer, the mechanism that updates each token's representation with a weighted mix of the tokens before it.

**Audio token** · Ch. 13
:   A short slice of sound compressed into a code that a model can receive or produce like a text token.

**Augmentation** · Ch. 5
:   Working with AI in which you and the AI shape and carry out the task together, turn by turn.

**Authorship (in copyright)** · Ch. 18
:   The legal status of having created the expression in a work; in U.S. law only a human can be an author.

**Automated decision** · Ch. 11
:   A decision in which an AI output triggers an action with no person in between.

**Automated workflow** · Ch. 14
:   A workflow whose steps software runs, along a path people fixed in advance.

**Automation bias** · Ch. 11
:   The tendency to over-rely on automated output, following it when it is wrong or missing what it did not flag.

**Automation (mode of working with AI)** · Ch. 5
:   Working with AI in which the AI carries out a task you define, and you check the output.

## B {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Bake-off** · Ch. 12
:   A side-by-side test of two or more tools, and where possible no AI, on the same part of a task.

**Base rate** · Ch. 16
:   How often the outcome actually occurs in a group.

**Baseline** · Ch. 1
:   An honest record of how you use AI at the start of the course, used to measure your progress.

**Benchmark** · Ch. 5
:   A standard test used to compare models.

**Bias audit** · Ch. 16
:   A structured test of whether a system's outputs or errors differ across groups, recorded with its method, counts and decisions.

**Bias (in an AI system)** · Ch. 16
:   A systematic difference in how a system's outputs or errors fall on different groups of people that disadvantages some of them.

**Bias (in generated output)** · Ch. 4
:   A systematic pattern in outputs that treats or represents people or groups unfairly.

**Bias Lifecycle** · Ch. 16
:   The book's four-phase picture of where bias can enter an AI system: data, model, use and feedback.

**Bias probe** · Ch. 16
:   A paired-input test used as A12's red-team probe.

**Biased labels** · Ch. 2
:   Labels that are wrong in one consistent direction, often because they record past decisions.

**Biometric data** · Ch. 15
:   Data about a person's body or behavior, such as a face, a voice, a fingerprint or the way someone walks.

**Black box** · Ch. 17
:   A system whose inputs and outputs can be seen but whose internal workings are not visible, or not understandable, to the people who use it or are affected by it.

## C {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Calibration gap** · Ch. 7 (also 8)
:   Your predicted score minus your actual score, across a set of answers; divided by the number of questions, your average confidence minus the share you got right. A positive gap means you were overconfident.

**Calibration (of a model)** · Ch. 8
:   How closely a model's stated confidence matches its accuracy.

**Calibration (of your own confidence)** · Ch. 7
:   How closely your confidence in your answers matches how often they are actually correct, across many answers.

**Calibration within groups (Deep)** · Ch. 16
:   A score means the same chance of the outcome in every group (a score of 0.7 means a 70% chance).

**Career narrative** · Ch. 20
:   A short argument to one named reader: where you are going, shown by three pieces of evidence.

**Career readiness** · Ch. 20
:   A foundation for showing the core competencies that prepare college graduates for success at work and for managing a career (NACE's definition, paraphrased).

**Case law** · Ch. 18
:   Court decisions that later courts follow.

**Chain-of-thought text** · Ch. 17
:   The step-by-step text a model produces before or with its answer, sometimes shown and sometimes hidden as reasoning tokens.

**Chance threshold** · Ch. 16
:   The smallest gap, in either direction, that chance alone reaches less than 1 time in 20 when both versions truly give the pattern 50% of the time.

**Cheap fake** · Ch. 13
:   Media manipulated without generative AI, such as a real photo with a false caption or date, a slowed-down video or a simple edit (Paris & Donovan, 2019).

**Check point** · Ch. 14
:   A point at which a person inspects an intermediate result before later steps build on it (not a saved restore point).

**Citation tracing** · Ch. 9
:   Following a claim from where you met it, hop by hop, to the place it first appeared, checking at each hop that the cited source says what the citing source claims.

**Claim** · Ch. 8
:   One statement in an output that you might rely on; marked checkable (it can be true or false) or not checkable as true or false (a judgment, recommendation or prediction).

**Class** · Ch. 2
:   One of the possible answers a classifier can give, such as "bolt" or "nut".

**Class imbalance** · Ch. 2
:   When one class has far fewer examples than the others.

**Closed captions** · Ch. 13
:   On-screen text of a video's speech and important sounds, which viewers can turn on or off.

**Cognitive offloading (Deep)** · Ch. 7
:   Using a tool or action to reduce the mental work a task requires, such as writing a note or using a calculator.

**Commission error** · Ch. 11
:   Following an automated output when it is wrong.

**Commitment (in a code of practice)** · Ch. 21
:   A line in your code that states an action you will take.

**Competency (career)** · Ch. 20
:   A capability that shows in what you do, not a topic you studied.

**Confabulation (Deep)** · Ch. 4
:   Another word for hallucination, used by some researchers and by NIST's Generative AI Profile: confidently stated but false content.

**Consistency check** · Ch. 8
:   Asking the same question in several new chats and comparing the answers.

**Constraint** · Ch. 5
:   A limit or a must-not in a prompt, such as a length, a source rule or an excluded topic.

**Content credentials** · Ch. 13
:   A provenance record attached to a file under the C2PA standard: signed statements about how the file was made and edited.

**Context engineering** · Ch. 6
:   Deciding what goes into a model's context window, from which layer, in what form and in what order, so that a task can be done well.

**Context layers** · Ch. 6
:   The separate sources of text that together fill a model's context window in one turn, each set by someone and at some time.

**Context loss** · Ch. 4
:   Output that ignores information or instructions the model was given.

**Context (prompt part)** · Ch. 5
:   The background a task needs that the tool cannot otherwise receive, such as figures, readers or source text.

**Context window** · Ch. 3
:   The space for everything a language model receives in one turn, measured in tokens; the response also counts toward it.

**Control group** · Ch. 1
:   In an experiment, the comparison group that does not receive the tool or treatment.

**Copyright** · Ch. 18
:   The legal right of the author of an original work to control copying, adaptation, distribution, public performance and public display; it arises automatically when the work is fixed and protects expression, not ideas or facts.

**Correction (of an article)** · Ch. 9
:   A notice that fixes part of a published article.

**Correlation** · Ch. 9
:   Two things varying together, which does not show that one causes the other.

**Counterfactual explanation** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation that names the smallest change to an input that would have changed the output.

**Criterion (in a decision matrix)** · Ch. 11
:   One of the things the options are judged on, with its own scale.

**Crutch (in learning with AI)** · Ch. 7
:   Help that does the part of the work you needed to do yourself, and that you keep depending on.

## D {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Data class** · Ch. 12
:   The category an institution assigns to information by how much harm its release could cause; UTD's policy names three: Public Data, Controlled Data and Confidential Data.

**Data gate** · Ch. 12
:   A check, made before any quality test, of whether a tool's data terms fit the class of the input.

**Data minimization** · Ch. 15
:   Sending only what a part of a task needs.

**Data terms** · Ch. 12
:   The parts of a tool's terms and its options that say what happens to what you type and upload.

**Data-flow map** · Ch. 15
:   A drawing of where one input goes once you send it: what goes in, where it is stored, who can see it, whether it is reused and where the output goes.

**Datasheet (for a dataset)** · Ch. 2 (also 17)
:   A document that records why a dataset was created, what it contains, how it was collected and labeled, and what it should not be used for (after Gebru et al., 2021).

**Data-to-Prediction Pipeline** · Ch. 2
:   The book's five-stage picture of how data becomes predictions: collect, label, train, predict, feedback.

**Dated note** · Ch. 21
:   A fact about a tool or a rule, written with the date it was true: "as of [month year]."

**Decision matrix** · Ch. 11
:   A table that lists options against the criteria they are judged on, each criterion with a scale and a weight.

**Decision owner** · Ch. 11
:   The named person or body who makes a decision and answers for its result.

**Decision support** · Ch. 11
:   AI output, such as a summary, an analysis, a score or a recommendation, that goes to a named person who decides and answers for the result.

**Decision-chain answer** · Ch. 20
:   An answer that gives five links: what you asked for, what the AI produced, what you kept, changed or rejected and why, how you checked, and who decided.

**Deep learning** · Ch. 2
:   Machine learning with many layers of simple computing units.

**Deepfake** · Ch. 13 (also 18)
:   Synthetic media that realistically shows a real person, or a real event, saying, doing or happening in a way that did not happen.

**Deepfake detector** · Ch. 13
:   A tool that gives a score for how likely an image, audio or video is to have been generated or altered by AI.

**Defense in depth** · Ch. 15
:   Several layers of defense, built to fail in different ways.

**De-identification** · Ch. 15
:   Removing names and obvious identifiers from data; a start, not a guarantee that the data is anonymous.

**Delegation Ladder** · Ch. 5
:   The book's arrangement of three ways of working with AI over a floor of no AI, ordered by how hard it is to check what the AI contributed before it takes effect.

**Deployer** · Ch. 18
:   An organization or person that uses an AI system in its own work, such as a company with a website chatbot.

**Desirable difficulty** · Ch. 7
:   A condition that makes learning feel harder and slower but improves long-term memory and use, provided you can meet it with effort.

**Difference-in-differences** · Ch. 1
:   A method that compares the change in one group with the change in a comparison group over the same period.

**Diffusion model** · Ch. 13
:   A generator that starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by a prompt, until an image (or audio or video) appears.

**Disaggregated evaluation** · Ch. 16
:   Reporting a system's performance separately for each group and subgroup instead of one overall number.

**Discipline** · Ch. 19
:   A field of study and work with its own questions, methods and standards.

**Discipline × Use Map** · Ch. 19
:   A table of fields against kinds of AI use in which each cell shows the default people point for a student's coursework (log review, check point, approval gate, keep with a person); this book's reading, which a field's rules and an instructor's policy override.

**Disclaimer** · Ch. 18
:   A notice that tries to limit responsibility, such as "AI responses may contain errors."

**Disclosure (of AI use)** · Ch. 10
:   Telling the people who rely on a message how AI was involved in making it, in a form and place they will see.

**Discriminative model** · Ch. 2
:   A model that learns the boundary between classes.

**Disparate impact (Deep)** · Ch. 18
:   A practice that falls more heavily on a protected group without a job-related reason.

**Documented (label)** · Ch. 4
:   A failure label for which the evidence shows the branch's defining feature.

**Domain tool** · Ch. 12
:   A tool built for one field, often given that field's records or documents.

**Done-criteria** · Ch. 14
:   Two or three checks that tell you whether a run succeeded.

**Drift (in a retelling)** · Ch. 9
:   A change in a claim as it is retold: a dropped caveat, a broadened claim, a cause read into a correlation, or a changed number.

**Drift (in a tool or model over time)** · Ch. 12
:   A change in how a named model or tool behaves on the same inputs over time, often after its provider updates it.

**Dry run** · Ch. 14
:   Running a whole workflow on test inputs with real effects switched off, before anyone relies on it.

**Dual authorization** · Ch. 15
:   A control under which two people must approve a payment or an account change.

## E {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Equal error rates** · Ch. 16
:   A fairness definition: the same share missed, and the same share flagged wrongly, in each group.

**Equal precision** · Ch. 16
:   A fairness definition: a flag means the same in each group; of the flagged, the same share were really positive (predictive parity).

**Equal selection rates** · Ch. 16
:   A fairness definition: the same share of each group is flagged (demographic parity).

**Error** · Ch. 2
:   How far a model's prediction is from the correct answer.

**Error compounding** · Ch. 14
:   The tendency for the chance of an error-free run to fall as steps are added, because each step is another chance for an error and later steps can build on earlier ones.

**Ethics washing (gloss, Ethics Lens)** · Ch. 21
:   A statement of good principles that makes a person or company look responsible without changing what they do.

**EU AI Act** · Ch. 18
:   Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the European Union's law on AI systems, which sets duties by level of risk.

**Evidence map** · Ch. 20
:   A table that lists each entry with the course outcome it shows, the NACE competency it gives evidence of, and where the checks are.

**Example** · Ch. 2
:   One item in a dataset, such as one photo or one email.

**Example-based explanation** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation that shows past cases a model treated as similar, or typical examples of each outcome.

**Executive order** · Ch. 18
:   A president's or governor's instructions to the government.

**Exfiltration** · Ch. 15
:   Getting data out of a system to an attacker.

**Expected calibration error (Deep)** · Ch. 8
:   The average gap between confidence and accuracy across confidence groups, giving larger groups more weight.

**Explainability** · Ch. 17
:   How far people can get reasons for a system's outputs that they can understand and use.

**Extrapolation (in labor-market forecasts; Deep)** · [VERIFY: chapter]
:   Estimating beyond what was measured, such as scaling survey answers up to a whole economy's jobs.

**Extrinsic hallucination** · Ch. 4
:   A hallucination that the input can neither support nor contradict; it adds something from elsewhere.

## F {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Fabricated citation** · Ch. 8
:   A citation to a work that does not exist.

**Failure (AI)** · Ch. 4
:   An output or action of an artificial intelligence (AI) system that does not do what the task needs.

**Failure Diary** · Ch. 4
:   A dated record of AI failures you met, each with the test that showed it, a label and likely causes.

**Failure Taxonomy Tree** · Ch. 4
:   The book's diagram that sorts AI failures into five branches, each with smaller leaves.

**Failure-to-harm chain** · Ch. 4
:   The links by which an AI error becomes a harm: the output is wrong, it is not checked before use, someone relies on it, and a loss follows.

**Fair use** · Ch. 18
:   A U.S. legal exception that permits some uses of a protected work without permission, decided case by case by weighing four factors.

**Fairness definition** · Ch. 16
:   A stated rule for which comparison between groups must come out equal.

**Faithfulness (of an explanation)** · Ch. 17
:   How accurately an explanation reflects the process that actually produced the output.

**False positive (of a detector)** · Ch. 10
:   A human-written text labeled AI-generated; the false-positive rate is the share of human texts labeled that way.

**False-positive rate (of a decision tool)** · Ch. 16
:   The share of people without the outcome who are flagged anyway.

**Feature** · Ch. 2
:   A measurable property of an input that a model uses, such as a pixel value or a house's size.

**Feature attribution** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation that assigns each input feature a share of the credit for an output, for one case or across many.

**Feedback loop (in an AI system)** · Ch. 16
:   A path by which a system's decisions become its next data, so a gap between groups can grow.

**FERPA** · Ch. 18
:   The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a U.S. law that protects students' education records.

**Fidelity (of a surrogate model)** · Ch. 17
:   How often a surrogate model gives the same output as the model it imitates.

**Field guide** · Ch. 19
:   A one-page summary, for one field, of what counts as correct and who can confirm it, which data is protected, which rules apply and who bears an error, plus typical uses and a career note.

**Fine-tuning** · Ch. 3
:   Extra training of an already trained model on a smaller, new set of texts or examples.

**Fit matrix** · Ch. 12
:   A table whose rows are the parts of a task and whose columns are the tools you tested plus no AI; each cell holds a fit decision, its rung and its reason.

**Fluent (output)** · Ch. 1
:   Smooth, confident, well-organized text that sounds expert, whether or not it is correct.

## G {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Gap instruction** · Ch. 6
:   A line in a prompt that says what to do when the material is not enough.

**Generation effect (learning)** · Ch. 7
:   The finding that information you produce yourself is remembered better than information you only read.

**Generative AI** · Ch. 2
:   AI that produces new content (text, images, audio or code); today built almost entirely with deep learning.

**Generative AI system** · Ch. 1
:   Software that produces new content, such as text, images or code, in response to an input.

**Ghostwriter** · Ch. 10
:   A person who writes a text that someone else signs.

**Global explanation** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation of how a model behaves across many cases, such as which features matter most overall.

**Governance (of AI)** · Ch. 18
:   The rules, roles and checks that decide how AI may be used and who is responsible for it.

**GRADE (Deep)** · Ch. 9
:   Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation: a system that rates the certainty of a body of health evidence, starting from study design and moving the rating down or up.

**Gradient descent** · Ch. 2
:   A training method that changes a model's settings in small steps that reduce the error.

**Gray literature** · Ch. 9
:   Material published outside journals and books, such as reports by governments, companies, charities and consulting firms.

## H {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Hallucination** · Ch. 1 (also 4)
:   Fluent output that is not supported by the model's input or by facts.

**Hard gate** · Ch. 14
:   A gate the system enforces outside the model, so the action cannot run unless a person acts, or cannot run at all.

**Hidden assumption** · Ch. 11
:   A choice built into data or an analysis that can change the result but is not stated.

**High-risk AI system (EU AI Act)** · Ch. 18
:   An AI system in a listed use, such as admission, grading, test monitoring or screening job applicants, or built into a regulated product.

**HIPAA** · Ch. 18
:   The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a U.S. law that protects health information held by health plans, most health-care providers and the companies that handle it for them.

**Holding** · Ch. 18
:   What a court decides in order to settle the case; it binds the courts below it and is only persuasive elsewhere.

**Homogenization** · Ch. 10
:   Becoming more alike; in writing, different writers' texts converging on the same phrasing.

## I {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Image token** · Ch. 13
:   A small square patch of an image, turned into numbers that a multimodal model receives the way it receives text tokens.

**Impact (of a risk)** · Ch. 15
:   How bad the consequences of a harmful event would be, rated low, medium or high by written anchors.

**Implementation intention (Deep)** · Ch. 21
:   A plan that links a goal you already hold to a cue in the world, in the form "if this situation arises, I will respond this way."

**Imputation** · Ch. 11
:   Filling a missing value with an estimate, such as the average of the other values.

**In-context example** · Ch. 5
:   A sample input with the output you want, placed in a prompt to show the pattern.

**Independent check** · Ch. 8
:   Evidence that no AI tool produced: a source with an author or publisher you can name, or your own recalculation or reasoning from known inputs.

**Inference** · Ch. 2
:   Using a trained model to produce an output for a new input.

**Inference (of personal attributes)** · Ch. 15
:   A model producing a likely personal detail that a text never states, such as a writer's location; not the same as Chapter 3's inference, running a model.

**Inferred (label)** · Ch. 4
:   A failure label for which the evidence does not show the branch's defining feature; drawn with a dashed border.

**Informed consent** · Ch. 19
:   A participant's agreement after being told what happens to their data.

**Infringement** · Ch. 18
:   Using a protected work in one of the ways copyright controls without permission or a legal exception.

**Institutional review board (IRB)** · Ch. 19
:   A committee that approves and oversees research with people.

**Instruction tuning** · Ch. 3
:   Further training on prompts paired with good responses written by people.

**Interpretability** · Ch. 17
:   How far a person can follow how a model turns inputs into outputs from the model itself.

**Interpretable model** · Ch. 17
:   A model whose decision process a person can follow from the model itself, such as a points scorecard, a short list of rules or a small decision tree; sometimes called a glass box.

**Intersectional subgroup** · Ch. 16
:   A group defined by two or more characteristics at once, such as darker-skinned women.

**Intrinsic hallucination** · Ch. 4
:   A hallucination that contradicts the input the model received: what you pasted, or what the system retrieved.

**Iteration** · Ch. 5
:   Improving a prompt by changing one thing at a time, predicting the effect, rerunning and scoring the result against your success criteria.

**Iteration log** · Ch. 5
:   A record of each prompt version: what changed, the prediction, the results of each run and the decision to keep or revert.

## J {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Jagged technological frontier** · Ch. 1
:   The uneven boundary between tasks an AI tool handles well and tasks it handles poorly, even among tasks that look equally hard.

**Jurisdiction** · Ch. 18
:   The area, such as a country, a state or a city, whose law applies.

## K {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Keyed questions** · Ch. 7
:   Questions that come with an answer key, such as a textbook's end-of-section or practice questions.

**Knowledge cutoff** · Ch. 3
:   The date after which no text was collected for a model's training.

## L {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Label** · Ch. 2
:   The correct answer attached to an example: a human decision or a recorded outcome.

**Labor-market churn (Deep)** · Ch. 20
:   Jobs created plus jobs displaced, as a share of the starting total.

**Labor-market forecast** · Ch. 20
:   An estimate of future jobs or skills, made by named people or organizations at a date.

**Large language model (LLM)** · Ch. 2 (also 3)
:   A generative model that produces text, trained on large amounts of text to predict the next token in a sequence.

**Lateral reading** · Ch. 9
:   Leaving a page early to see what outside sources say about who is behind it.

**Law** · Ch. 18
:   Rules made by a government and enforced by courts or agencies.

**Leaderboard (Deep)** · Ch. 12
:   A ranking of models by benchmarks or by crowd votes.

**Learning (durable)** · Ch. 7
:   A lasting change in what you can do without help, shown later and in new situations.

**Learning from human feedback** · Ch. 3
:   A training stage in which people rank responses, a separate scoring model is trained on their rankings, and the settings move toward responses that score higher.

**Learning rate** · Ch. 2
:   The size of each adjustment step in gradient descent.

**Least privilege** · Ch. 14
:   Giving each tool and account only the access its step needs, for only as long as it is needed.

**Lethal trifecta** · Ch. 15
:   Willison's (2025) name for a system that combines three legs, access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to send data out, which together allow data theft.

**Liability** · Ch. 18
:   Legal responsibility to make up for harm or to pay a penalty.

**Liar's dividend** · Ch. 13
:   The benefit a person gains by dismissing real recordings as fake when fakes are common (Chesney & Citron, 2019).

**License** · Ch. 18
:   Permission to use something on stated conditions.

**Licensure** · Ch. 19
:   Permission from a state body to practice a profession.

**Likelihood (of a risk)** · Ch. 15
:   How probable a harmful event is, rated low, medium or high by written anchors.

**Listwise deletion** · Ch. 11
:   Deleting every row that has a missing value, so the analysis uses complete rows only.

**Local explanation** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation of why a model produced one output for one case.

**Local model** · Ch. 12
:   An open-weight model run on hardware that you or your institution control, so your input need not go to the model's provider.

**Lock-in** · Ch. 12
:   The effort and cost that keep you on a tool after a better fit appears.

**Log (of an agent run)** · Ch. 14
:   A record the system writes as it runs of every plan, tool call, observation, approval and stop, with times.

## M {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Machine learning** · Ch. 2
:   The part of AI in which a system finds rules (patterns) from examples instead of having them written by people.

**Memory (product feature)** · Ch. 3
:   A product feature that saves notes about a user, or draws on past chats, and adds them to later conversations; it adds text and does not train the model.

**Meta-analysis** · Ch. 9
:   A study that combines the results of many studies statistically into one estimate.

**Metacognition** · Ch. 7
:   Knowing about and monitoring your own thinking and learning.

**Metadata** · Ch. 13
:   Data about a file, such as when, where and with what it was made.

**Miss rate** · Ch. 16
:   The share of real cases not flagged (one minus recall).

**Missing at random, MAR (Deep)** · Ch. 11
:   Values are missing for a reason that depends only on things you did observe.

**Missing completely at random, MCAR (Deep)** · Ch. 11
:   Values are missing for a reason that has nothing to do with any data.

**Missing not at random, MNAR (Deep)** · Ch. 11
:   Values are missing for a reason that depends on the missing value itself.

**Missing value** · Ch. 11
:   An empty cell or field where a value should be.

**Mitigation** · Ch. 15
:   A change that lowers a risk's likelihood, its impact or both; this book uses four kinds: avoid, reduce, detect, accept.

**Mitigation (of bias)** · Ch. 16
:   A change meant to reduce a measured bias.

**Modality** · Ch. 13
:   A kind of data, such as text, images, audio or video.

**Model** · Ch. 1 (also 2)
:   A set of learned settings (parameters) that turns an input into an output; in an AI tool, the part that produces the output from your prompt. (Informal in Ch. 1, formal in Ch. 2.)

**Model card** · Ch. 17 (also 19)
:   A short document published with a model that states what it is for and not for, how it was evaluated, including results by group where relevant, and its known limits (after Mitchell et al., 2019).

**Multimodal model** · Ch. 13
:   A model that receives or produces more than one kind of data, such as text, images, audio or video.

**Multiple imputation (Deep)** · Ch. 11
:   Filling each missing value several times with plausible values, analyzing each completed dataset and pooling the results with their extra uncertainty.

## N {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Net job growth (Deep)** · Ch. 20
:   The expected change in the size of the workforce: jobs created minus jobs displaced.

**Next-token prediction** · Ch. 3
:   Producing text one token at a time in four steps: split the text into tokens, score every possible next token, pick one, add it and repeat.

**No-AI baseline** · Ch. 12
:   The time a part of a task takes you without any AI tool, done well enough to meet your criteria.

**Noisy labels** · Ch. 2
:   Labels that are wrong at random, in no particular direction.

## O {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Omission error** · Ch. 11
:   Missing a problem because an automated system did not flag it.

**Omitted key result** · Ch. 9
:   A finding that changes the picture but is missing from a summary.

**Open access** · Ch. 9
:   Free to read online.

**Open-weight model** · Ch. 12
:   A model whose settings (parameters), called its weights, can be downloaded and run under a license.

**Option** · Ch. 3
:   A control a user can change, such as temperature or search on or off; unlike the model's settings (parameters), it is not learned.

**Opt-out (text and data mining) (Deep)** · Ch. 18
:   A rights holder's machine-readable reservation that excludes its works from text and data mining under EU law.

**Oral defense** · Ch. 20
:   A short, live explanation of your work followed by questions, in which you show that you own it.

**Outdated information** · Ch. 1 (also 4)
:   Output that was once correct but no longer is, because of a training-data cutoff or stale search results.

**Out-of-band check** · Ch. 13
:   Confirming a request or a claim through a separate channel you already trust, not one the message provides.

**Output** · Ch. 1
:   What an AI tool produces in response to a prompt.

**Output format** · Ch. 5
:   The shape the output should take, such as a table, a list or a word limit, chosen so it can be checked.

**Outside source** · Ch. 9
:   A source not written or paid for by whoever is behind the page you are checking.

**Outsourcing** · Ch. 1
:   AI use that replaces the thinking an assignment or task requires of you.

**Overconfidence** · Ch. 1 (also 4)
:   Output stated with more certainty than the evidence supports.

**Overfitting** · Ch. 2
:   When a model fits its training examples so closely that it stops improving, or gets worse, on new examples.

**Overreliance** · Ch. 7
:   Relying on an AI tool's output more than the task or the evidence warrants, so that your own checking or skill-building drops out.

**Own evidence (in a code of practice)** · Ch. 21
:   Something from your own work that shows why a line matters to you, such as a Failure Diary entry, an assignment result or a lab record; a rule counts only together with it.

**Ownership (of a text)** · Ch. 10
:   Having decided what a text says, and being able to explain, defend and stand behind every sentence in it and its consequences; not the same as legal authorship.

## P {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Paired-input test** · Ch. 16
:   A test that runs inputs identical except for one cue linked to a group, many times each, counts the outputs by a rule fixed before any run, and compares the counts.

**Parameter** · Ch. 2
:   One of the learned settings inside a model; training adjusts parameters.

**Peer review** · Ch. 9
:   The checking of a research manuscript by a few experts in the field, at a journal editor's request, before publication.

**Peer swap test** · Ch. 5
:   Someone else runs your prompt without your explanation and scores the output against your criteria, to reveal what was in your head but not in the prompt.

**Peer test** · Ch. 19
:   A test in which a person from another field runs your prototype on an input of their choosing, within its stated scope and with only your instructions, and records where it confused them or failed.

**People point** · Ch. 19
:   A place where a person checks AI work (Chapter 14: approval gate, check point, stop point); on the Discipline × Use Map, a use's default level: log review, check point, approval gate or keep with a person.

**Percentage point** · Ch. 1
:   The simple difference between two percentages (for example, 84% minus 65% is 19 percentage points).

**Performance (during practice)** · Ch. 7
:   How well you do a task while practicing, often with help; it can differ from what you have learned.

**Perplexity (Deep)** · Ch. 10
:   Roughly, how unlikely a language model's scores make each next word; low perplexity means the words are easy to predict.

**Personal AI code of practice** · Ch. 21
:   A short set of commitments you choose for how you will use AI in your own work, each written so that you recognize when it applies, with a date to review it.

**Personal data** · Ch. 15
:   Information about an identified or identifiable person (also called personally identifiable information, PII).

**Placeholder** · Ch. 6
:   A marked slot in a template, such as {NOTES} or {DATE}, that you replace with new material each time you use it.

**Planted fault** · Ch. 14
:   An error put into one step of a dry run on purpose, to see whether a check point, gate or stop point catches it.

**Policy (of an organization)** · Ch. 18
:   The written rules of a course, university or employer.

**Population** · Ch. 2
:   Everything a model will meet in the real world.

**Portfolio Anatomy** · Ch. 20
:   The book's diagram of a portfolio as an argument: a career narrative and an evidence map backed by entries (artifact, revision trace, verification trail, declaration), a reflection, a code of practice and an oral defense.

**Portfolio (course sense)** · Ch. 20
:   A selection of your work, each piece with the evidence of how you made and checked it, presented for a reader outside the course.

**Portfolio entry** · Ch. 20
:   A short account of one piece of work for an outside reader: the situation and task, what you did, what the AI did, how you checked, the result and one limit.

**Post-hoc explanation** · Ch. 17
:   An explanation produced after a model is built, by a separate method that studies the model's inputs and outputs.

**Precision** · Ch. 2
:   Of the cases a model flagged, the share that were really positive.

**Predictive policing (Deep)** · Ch. 16
:   Software that sends patrols to areas where past records show more crime.

**Preprint** · Ch. 9
:   A research manuscript posted publicly before peer review.

**Pretraining** · Ch. 3
:   The first stage of training a language model: self-supervised learning on very large collections of text, in which the settings are adjusted so that the real next token gets a higher score.

**Primary source** · Ch. 8
:   The original record a claim comes from: the study, the dataset, the law, the court record, the official page of the organization that sets the rule.

**Probability distribution** · Ch. 3
:   A set of chances for all possible outcomes that add up to 100%.

**Probe** · Ch. 3
:   A small test of a model's behavior with four parts: prediction, prompt, result and conclusion.

**Process evidence** · Ch. 10
:   The record of how you wrote: notes, earlier drafts, version history, revision trace, declaration, and your ability to explain your choices.

**Productivity (in a study)** · Ch. 1
:   A defined measure of output per unit of time, such as issues resolved per hour.

**Professional code of ethics** · Ch. 21
:   A statement of principles a profession sets for its members.

**Prohibited practice (EU AI Act)** · Ch. 18
:   An AI use the EU AI Act bans, such as inferring people's emotions from their faces or voices at work or in education.

**Project space** · Ch. 6
:   A workspace in a tool where chosen files and instructions are added to every conversation started inside it.

**Prompt** · Ch. 1
:   The input you give an AI tool.

**Prompt chain** · Ch. 6
:   A fixed sequence of prompts that you run one after another, where each step's output becomes the next step's input and you check the result between steps.

**Prompt injection** · Ch. 4
:   Text that acts as an instruction to an AI system against its owner's intent; direct when a user types it, indirect when it is hidden in content the system retrieves.

**Prompt library** · Ch. 6
:   A personal or shared collection of tested prompt templates, each recorded with when to use it, what it was tested on and how it has changed.

**Prompt template** · Ch. 6
:   A prompt written for a recurring task, with fixed parts that stay the same each time and placeholders for the parts that change.

**Prompt version** · Ch. 6
:   A numbered, dated state of a prompt or template, recorded with what changed and what it was tested on.

**Protected characteristic** · Ch. 16
:   A characteristic, such as race or sex, that anti-discrimination law says decisions such as hiring must not be based on.

**Prototype** · Ch. 19
:   The smallest working version of a workflow, built so that someone can run it, check it and change it.

**Provenance** · Ch. 13
:   A record of where a piece of content came from and how it was changed.

**Provider** · Ch. 12 (also 18)
:   The company or institution that runs an AI tool.

**Provider (EU AI Act and Texas law)** · Ch. 12 (also 18)
:   The organization that builds an AI system or puts it on the market (called a developer in Texas law).

**Proxy** · Ch. 2
:   A clue that stands in for something else, such as a word linked to gender.

**Proxy label** · Ch. 11
:   A recorded outcome used as the label because it is easy to measure, standing in for the outcome you actually care about.

**Public domain** · Ch. 18
:   Works that copyright no longer protects, or never did.

**Pushback test** · Ch. 4
:   A probe that challenges a correct answer to see whether the output changes to agree with you.

## Q {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Qualifying risk** · Ch. 15
:   A risk that needs a full mitigation plan in A12: its impact is high, or both its likelihood and its impact are at least medium.

**Quasi-identifier** · Ch. 15
:   A detail that is harmless alone but identifying together with others, such as ZIP code, sex and date of birth.

## R {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Random assignment** · Ch. 1
:   Using chance to decide who receives a tool, so groups are alike on average in everything else.

**Reasoning tokens** · Ch. 3
:   Extra tokens some tools produce before the answer, sometimes hidden; they are made in the same way as other tokens and count toward context and cost.

**Recall** · Ch. 2
:   Of the real cases of a class, the share the model caught (the score on the smallest class in Ch. 2).

**Recombination** · Ch. 4
:   Joining patterns learned from true text into a statement that is false.

**Recourse** · Ch. 17
:   A counterfactual change that a person can actually make.

**Redaction** · Ch. 20
:   Removing or blacking out information so it cannot be read.

**Red-teaming** · Ch. 15
:   Testing a system the way an attacker would, with permission, to find weaknesses first.

**Registration (copyright)** · Ch. 18
:   Recording a work with the U.S. Copyright Office; optional, but needed before suing over a U.S. work.

**Regulation** · Ch. 18
:   A rule made by an agency, or a law adopted by the European Union.

**Regulation Map** · Ch. 18
:   This book's nine-box picture of where the rules for an AI use come from: law by jurisdiction (EU, U.S. federal law and executive policy, states, cities), agreements (terms, licenses, contracts) and your organization's policy.

**Re-identification** · Ch. 15
:   Linking quasi-identifiers with another record, such as a voter list, to learn who a person in a dataset is.

**Remaining uncertainty** · Ch. 8
:   What you could not check, and why; recorded with every verdict.

**Representation harm** · Ch. 16
:   Harm that stereotypes, demeans or leaves out a group in what people see and read.

**Research-report tool** · Ch. 9
:   A system that runs many searches, retrieves many pages and produces a long report with citations; often marketed as "deep research."

**Residual risk** · Ch. 15
:   The risk that remains after mitigation.

**Re-test trigger** · Ch. 12
:   An event that should make you test a fit again, such as a model update or retirement, a change in price or terms, a new kind of input, or a change of job or school.

**Retraction** · Ch. 9
:   The withdrawal of a published article because of serious error or misconduct.

**Retrieval** · Ch. 3
:   A system's search of a collection, such as the web or a set of files, that adds the passages it finds to the context window.

**Retrieval practice (learning)** · Ch. 7
:   Recalling information from your own memory, for example by self-testing, which strengthens it more than restudying. Not the same as retrieval in an AI system (Ch. 3).

**Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** · Ch. 3
:   Producing a response with retrieved passages added to the context window.

**Reversal curse** · Ch. 3
:   The finding that a model trained on "A is B" often fails to answer "B is A" (Berglund et al., 2024).

**Reverse image search** · Ch. 13
:   Searching with an image, instead of words, to find where it or similar images appear online, including its earliest version.

**Reversible action** · Ch. 14
:   An action whose effect can be undone at little cost, such as a draft, an item in a cart or a change in a test copy.

**Review date** · Ch. 21
:   The date by which you reread your whole code and keep, revise or retire each line.

**Revision evidence** · Ch. 20
:   The record, for one artifact, of the before, the after, the reason for the change and the check behind it.

**Revision trace** · Ch. 10
:   A record of versions, from your notes or first draft to the tool's draft to your final version, with what changed, who or what proposed it, and why.

**Right (in the rules-and-rights risk)** · Ch. 18
:   Something a law or an agreement lets a person control or claim, such as copyright in their work or privacy of their records.

**Right to contest** · Ch. 17
:   Being able to challenge a decision before a person who can review and change it.

**Risk** · Ch. 15
:   A combination of how likely a harmful event is and how bad its consequences would be (after NIST, 2023).

**Risk Heat Map** · Ch. 15
:   Signature 10: a 3-by-3 grid of likelihood by impact on which each risk is placed, with its evidence marked documented or inferred; risks in the high-impact row need a mitigation or a named owner.

**Risk owner** · Ch. 15
:   The person who agrees in writing to carry a risk.

**Risk register** · Ch. 15
:   A list of risks with their ratings and evidence.

**Role (prompt part)** · Ch. 5
:   The voice or perspective the output takes; who will read the output belongs in the context.

**Rule-based system** · Ch. 2
:   A system that follows rules written by people.

**Rules-and-rights risk** · Ch. 18
:   An A12 risk written as "risk of breaking [a named rule] or of [a named person] losing [a named right]," with the rule's own text as evidence.

**Runaway feedback loop (Deep)** · Ch. 16
:   A feedback loop in which a system keeps being sent back to where it already looked, whatever the true rate.

**Rung needed** · Ch. 9
:   The rung of the source ladder that your purpose and the stakes require for a claim.

## S {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Sample** · Ch. 2
:   The examples we actually have.

**Sampling bias** · Ch. 2
:   A systematic difference between the sample and the population.

**Sampling (of tokens)** · Ch. 3
:   Picking the next token according to the model's scores (not the same as a sample of examples in Chapter 2).

**Sandbox** · Ch. 14
:   A separate test copy where changes do not reach real data or people.

**Scaffold** · Ch. 7
:   Temporary support that lets you do what you cannot yet do alone, withdrawn as you improve.

**Scope of practice** · Ch. 19
:   What the members of a licensed profession may do.

**Secondary source** · Ch. 9
:   A source that reports on or interprets primary sources, such as a review article, a textbook or a news story about a study.

**Security vulnerability (AI)** · Ch. 4
:   A weakness that lets someone make an AI system act against its owner's intent or reveal what it should not.

**Selection rate** · Ch. 16
:   The share of a group that a tool flags.

**Self-supervised learning** · Ch. 2
:   Learning from examples whose answer is hidden in the data itself, such as the next word in a sentence.

**Sensitive data** · Ch. 15
:   Personal data that can do special harm if exposed, such as biometric, health or location data.

**Sensitivity analysis (Deep, missing data)** · Ch. 11
:   Assuming the missing values were somewhat higher or lower than the fill and checking whether the conclusion survives.

**Sensitivity check** · Ch. 11
:   Changing one choice in an analysis, such as a weight or the handling of a blank, to see whether the result changes.

**Shortcut** · Ch. 2
:   A clue that goes with the label in the training data but is irrelevant to the task.

**Simpson's paradox** · Ch. 11
:   A pattern in a total that weakens or even reverses inside the groups that make it up.

**Social engineering** · Ch. 13
:   Manipulating people, rather than breaking into systems, to get them to give money, access or information.

**Socratic questioning** · Ch. 7
:   Teaching by asking questions that lead the learner to reason the answer out.

**Soft gate** · Ch. 14
:   An instruction in the context asking the model to ask first or not to act; the model receives it as text and may not follow it.

**Source ladder** · Ch. 9
:   The book's four-rung picture of how directly a source records a claim, judged from the source alone: 4, it is the record of this claim; 3, it cites the specific record or records a narrower part of the claim; 2, it names a source too vaguely to find; 1, it gives no source.

**Spacing (spaced practice)** · Ch. 7
:   Spreading study of the same material over separate sessions instead of massing it in one.

**Staggered rollout** · Ch. 1
:   Introducing a tool to groups at different times, which lets researchers compare groups with and without it.

**Stakeholder** · Ch. 16
:   Everyone affected by a decision, including people who never use the tool.

**Stakes (of a claim)** · Ch. 8
:   What would be lost, by you or by someone else, if the claim were wrong.

**Standing instructions** · Ch. 6
:   Instructions you write once, in a tool's options or a project, that the tool adds to every conversation in that scope.

**Stated confidence** · Ch. 8
:   The certainty an output expresses in words or numbers, such as "I'm 95% sure" or "definitely."

**Statute** · Ch. 18
:   A law passed by a legislature.

**Stock phrase** · Ch. 10
:   A ready-made phrase used by many writers, such as "I am writing to inform you."

**Stop point** · Ch. 14
:   A condition at which a run halts and hands control back to a person, such as a step, time or spending limit, an error, or an unexpected result.

**Success criteria** · Ch. 5
:   Checks, written in advance, that an output must pass to count as good; each can be scored met, partly met or not met.

**Summary fidelity** · Ch. 9
:   How closely a summary's claims match what the original supports.

**Supervised learning** · Ch. 2
:   Learning from examples that each come with a correct answer (label).

**Surrogate model** · Ch. 17
:   A simpler model trained to imitate a complex one, often to explain it.

**Sycophancy** · Ch. 4
:   Output that agrees with your stated view even when the evidence points the other way.

**Synthetic media** · Ch. 13 (also 18)
:   Images, audio or video generated or substantially altered by AI.

**System card** · Ch. 17
:   A provider's document about a released AI system, describing its evaluations, known risks and safety measures.

**System prompt** · Ch. 3
:   Instructions from a tool's provider or developer that are added to the context window, usually unseen by the user.

**Systematic review** · Ch. 9
:   A review that searches for every study on a question with a written plan.

## T {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Task frame** · Ch. 5
:   A short statement of a task's goal, audience, success criteria, limits and what stays with you, written before the first prompt.

**Task (prompt part)** · Ch. 5
:   What you want done: an action and what it acts on. The one part every prompt needs.

**Task–tool fit** · Ch. 12
:   How well one tool, used in one way, meets one task's success criteria within your limits of data and cost, on a given date.

**Temperature** · Ch. 3
:   An option that changes how often less likely tokens are picked; it does not change the model's settings.

**Terms of service** · Ch. 18
:   The contract a provider sets for using its tool.

**Tertiary source** · Ch. 9
:   A source that collects and condenses secondary ones, such as an encyclopedia, an index or a study guide.

**Test inputs** · Ch. 5
:   A small set of different inputs a prompt is tried on (typical, different, edge) to see whether it works beyond one case.

**Test set** · Ch. 2
:   Labeled examples kept away from training and used only to score the model.

**Token** · Ch. 3
:   A unit of text (a word, part of a word, or a symbol) that a language model receives and produces.

**Tokenizer** · Ch. 3
:   A program that splits text into tokens and gives each token a number.

**Tone** · Ch. 10
:   The attitude a message conveys toward its reader and topic, such as formal, warm or brief.

**Tool use** · Ch. 3
:   A model producing a request to run other software, such as a calculator or a search engine, whose result is added to the context window.

**Total cost of use** · Ch. 12
:   The price of a tool, plus usage limits, the time spent checking outputs, the time spent learning the tool, what you give up in data, and the cost of switching later.

**Trademark** · Ch. 18
:   A word, name, logo or other sign that identifies who offers goods or services, protected for the business that uses it in trade, whoever designed it.

**Training data** · Ch. 2
:   The examples a model learns from.

**Training set** · Ch. 2
:   The labeled examples used to train a model.

**Transcription (speech recognition)** · Ch. 13
:   Turning spoken audio into written text.

**Transformative (use)** · Ch. 18
:   A use that adds a new purpose rather than standing in for the original.

**Transformer (Deep)** · Ch. 3
:   The model architecture, introduced in 2017, on which most of today's large language models are built (as of October 2026).

**Transparency duty** · Ch. 18
:   A duty to tell people they are dealing with AI, or that content was generated or altered by AI.

**Transparency (of an AI system)** · Ch. 17 (also 18)
:   Openness about a system: whether it is used, what it is for, what data and logic it relies on, how it was tested and who answers for it.

**Trial court** · Ch. 18
:   The court that hears a case first; in the U.S. federal system, a district court.

**Trigger (in a code of practice)** · Ch. 21
:   The observable situation that tells you a commitment applies now.

**Trigger test** · Ch. 21
:   Three questions a line must pass: would you notice the moment at the time, could you or someone else trace afterward that you acted, and does the reason point to your own evidence?

**Trust boundary** · Ch. 15
:   The line past which your data is handled under someone else's rules.

**Tutor mode** · Ch. 7
:   A way of using an AI tool in which it is set up to respond with questions and hints and to wait for your attempts, instead of giving answers.

**Two-part rule** · Ch. 16
:   A gap is a finding only if (1) the test was fair (one change, a fixed counting rule, one tool, fresh chats, the same number of runs per version, at least 10) and (2) the gap is at least the chance threshold; otherwise it is a lead.

## U {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Uncertainty signal** · Ch. 8
:   A feature of an output that makes an error more or less likely without settling whether a claim is true.

**Use decision** · Ch. 9
:   Your choice of how to use a source (rely on it, use it with a caveat, use it only as a lead, or do not use it); "rely on it" needs both a rung that meets your need and nothing in your outside sources that gives you reason to distrust who is behind it.

## V {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Verdict** · Ch. 8
:   A judgment on the book's five-point scale: supported (the evidence says what the claim says); partly supported (part holds, part does not or is missing); unsupported (no evidence for it at the stage you reached: nothing found, or the source does not say it); contradicted (the evidence says otherwise); cannot verify (the evidence exists or may exist, but you cannot reach it).

**Verification** · Ch. 8
:   Checking a claim against evidence that no AI tool produced.

**Verification authority** · Ch. 19
:   The source or person a field accepts as able to confirm a result: a primary record, a standard, a replication, a licensed professional or a trained specialist.

**Verification cost** · Ch. 12
:   The time and effort needed to confirm that an output meets your criteria.

**Verification Funnel** · Ch. 8
:   The book's diagram of three checks a claim can pass through (an independent check, the primary source, an expert), each outside the tool, taken only as far as the stakes require.

**Verification protocol** · Ch. 13
:   Rules you write in advance for when and how you check media and media-borne requests before you act on them.

**Verification trail** · Ch. 20
:   The record of checks behind a result, with the sources or recalculations used, the verdicts reached and what remained uncertain.

**Vertical reading** · Ch. 9
:   Judging a page by its own look and its own claims.

**Voice and ownership spectrum** · Ch. 10
:   The book's five positions for a use of AI in writing, ordered by how much of the wording a tool supplies: your words only, AI as reader (you write every change), AI as editor (you accept or reject the tool's wording), AI as co-drafter, AI as author (sent as is).

**Voice cloning** · Ch. 13 (also 18)
:   Using AI to produce new speech that imitates a particular person's voice from samples of it.

**Voice (in writing)** · Ch. 10
:   The impression of a writer that a reader forms from the writer's choices of words, sentence shapes, stance and what to include.

## W {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Watermark (media)** · Ch. 13
:   A pattern, visible or hidden, that a tool places in the image, audio or video it produces, which a matching detector can later test for.

**Watermark (text; Deep)** · Ch. 10
:   A hidden statistical pattern in the tokens a provider's model favors, which a matching tool can later test for.

**Weight (in a decision matrix)** · Ch. 11
:   How much a criterion counts toward the total.

**Workflow** · Ch. 14
:   A fixed sequence of steps for a task, run by people, by software or by both.

**Workflow blueprint** · Ch. 14
:   A written design of a workflow: its steps, who or what runs each, its actions, people points, permissions, log plan and dry-run results.

**Workflow card** · Ch. 19
:   This book's five-field version of a model card for a student workflow: not for, for, tested on, results, and limits and safeguards.

**Write first** · Ch. 10
:   Putting down what you want to say, in notes or a rough draft, before you ask a tool for anything.
